### Contributing guidelines

- [X] I have read [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

### Module(s)

mini.ai

### Question

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c41390b6-9563-4f2e-b907-f3da51b50657

```lua
local MiniAi = require("mini.ai")

MiniAi.setup({
  custom_textobjects = {
    F = MiniAi.gen_spec.treesitter({ a = "@function.outer", i = "@function.inner" }),
  },
})

vim.keymap.set("n", "gj", function()
  MiniAi.move_cursor("left", "a", "F", { search_method = "next" })
end, {})
vim.keymap.set("n", "gk", function()
  MiniAi.move_cursor("left", "a", "F", { search_method = "prev" })
end, {})

local function outer1()
  local function inner1() end
  local function inner2() end
  inner1()
  inner2()
end

function outer2()
  local function inner1() end
  local function inner2() end
  inner1()
  inner2()
end

local function outer3() end

outer1()
outer2()
outer3()
```

Press:

```
15j
6 * gj
gk
gk
```

I'd like to hear other opinions, but to me it feels unintuitive. Personally, I'd prefer the `nvim-treesitter-textobject` behavior, where both directions follow the same jump chain. Maybe `cover_or_next` and `cover_or_prev` should stay the way they are, while `next` and `prev` follow `nvim-treesitter-textobject`-like approach instead. But my brain has been malfunctioning lately, so I'm not entirely sure.

comment_data.body:
It seems to work as expected and is mostly the matter of choosing the correct distance approach when computing which span is the closest.

It was a long time ago, but I remember trying to find the most intuitive behavior and [the current one](https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim/blob/cad365c212fb1e332cb93fa8f72697125799d00a/lua/mini/ai.lua#L1813-L1824) was the one. The basic idea is to find the region for a textobject match that is "closest in that direction". This means that:
- For "next" it chooses a region with its closest *left/start* position that is *after* the cursor. This is true for all six `gj` cases, even the ones nested in other regions.
- For "prev" it chooses a region with its closest *right/end* position that is *before* the cursor. This is true for all `gk` cases, since every one moves cursor to the matching region's start. If the mapping was for `"right"` side, it would have traversed all the matches from the `gj` case, just landing at their ends.

I don't think there is a universally good answer to this, apart from maybe a more comprehensive set of mappings. Like all combinations of `[` / `{` / `]` / `}` that would mean something like "forward to the left side" or "backward to the right side". This feels a bit too much for 'mini.ai', but I have some similar ideas for planned 'mini.hierarchy'.

reply_data.body:
I'm doing jumping with dot-repeat support via `nvim-treesitter-textobjects` (part of the code):

```lua
  vim.keymap.set({ "n", "x", "o" }, "]]" .. key, function() MiniAi.move_cursor("left", ai_type, id, { search_method = "next" }) end, { desc = desc })
  vim.keymap.set({ "n", "x", "o" }, "[[" .. key, function() MiniAi.move_cursor("left", ai_type, id, { search_method = "prev" }) end, { desc = desc })
  vim.keymap.set({ "n", "x", "o" }, "][" .. key, function() MiniAi.move_cursor("right", ai_type, id,{ search_method =  "next" }) end, { desc = desc })
  vim.keymap.set({ "n", "x", "o" }, "[]" .. key, function() MiniAi.move_cursor("right", ai_type, id,{ search_method =  "prev" }) end, { desc = desc })
```

For example, if I use `]]a` (argument) followed by `;` and press it more times than needed, then try to jump back with `[[a` (`,`), it can skip over a few entries instead of returning to the expected position.

I've partially mitigated this by using `nvim-treesitter-textobjects` for jumping treesitter stuff, but that doesn't solve the issue when it comes to patterns. I kinda understand the underlying logic, but it still feels a bit odd for my workflow. I guess I need to press `[]a` followed by `g[a`.

Anyway, thanks for your answer.
